blocks.content: CASSANDRA
I woke up at two-something with Winston half under the blanket and my heart beating wrong.
I know this feeling. I've known it long enough that it doesn't scare me the way it used to. It's just a thing my body does. I breathe the way they taught me.
In for four.
Hold.
Out for six.
Again.
Again.

The room was dark except for a thin line of moonlight across the floor. Down the hall the house creaked. My parents were asleep. Maya probably wasn't — she doesn't sleep the same way anymore. She's always listening for something she won't name.
I reached for the small bottle on my nightstand. Looked at it for a second. I do that sometimes — just look at it. It's such a small thing to mean so much.
I took what I needed and lay back and waited.
My breathing evened out. Sleep didn't come back right away.

So instead I thought about the park. The fountain that tried. The guy who retied a shoe that wasn't untied. The way he'd looked at his canvas like he was trying to tell the truth and hoping nobody noticed.
I wondered if he'd finished it.
I wondered if he'd made the fountain less sad.
And then I thought — I wonder if I'll see him again — and I caught myself mid-thought because that is exactly the kind of wondering that starts small and gets expensive.
Hope with a specific face attached is where it always gets complicated.

I turned onto my side and held Winston against my chest and smiled into the dark anyway, because I've never been great at telling myself not to feel things. It's my worst quality. It is also, sometimes, my best one.
Just a story.
But my heart, stubborn and stupid and very much alive, whispered back:
Maybe the beginning of one.
